title: The Story of the Three Calenders, Sons of Kings, and of Five Ladies of Baghdad
paragraphs: In the reign of Caliph Haroun-al-Raschid, there lived in Baghdad a porter who, humble as his work was, had a sharp mind and good sense. One morning he was sitting in his usual spot with his basket in front of him, waiting for someone to hire him, when a tall young woman in a long muslin veil walked up and said, “Pick up your basket and come with me.” Delighted with her looks and her voice, the porter jumped up at once, hoisted his basket onto his head and followed her, telling himself as he went, “What a happy day! What a lucky meeting!”

Soon the lady stopped at a closed door and knocked. An old man with a long white beard opened it, and without a word she held out some money. The old man seemed to know what she wanted. He disappeared into the house and came back with a large jar of wine, which the porter set in his basket. Then the lady motioned for him to follow, and off they went.

Her next stop was a fruit and flower shop, where she bought a great quantity of apples, apricots, peaches and other fruit, together with lilies, jasmine and all kinds of fragrant plants. From there she went to a butcher, a grocer and a poulterer, until the porter finally cried out in despair, “My good lady, if you’d only told me you meant to buy enough food to supply a town, I’d have brought a horse, or better, a camel.” The lady laughed and told him she wasn’t finished. She picked out a range of perfumes and spices at a druggist’s shop, and then stopped in front of a magnificent palace, where she knocked softly at the door. The porteress who opened it was so beautiful that the man was dazzled, and all the more astonished because he could plainly see she was no slave. The lady who had brought him stood watching him with amusement, until the porteress said, “Why don’t you come in, sister? This poor man is so weighed down he’s about to drop.”

When they were both inside, the door was bolted, and the three of them went into a large courtyard ringed by an open-work gallery. At one end was a platform, and on the platform stood an amber throne held up by four ebony columns and decorated with pearls and diamonds. In the middle of the courtyard was a marble basin, filled with water that flowed from the mouth of a golden lion.

The porter looked around, taking in and admiring everything. But what caught his attention most was a third lady seated on the throne, who was even more beautiful than the other two. From the respect the others showed her, he guessed she was the eldest, and he was right. Her name was Zobeida, the porteress was called Sadie, and the housekeeper was Amina. At a word from Zobeida, Sadie and Amina took the basket from the porter, who was glad to be rid of the weight, and when it was emptied they paid him generously for his trouble. But instead of picking up his basket and leaving, the man hung about, until Zobeida asked what he was waiting for and whether he expected more money. “Oh, madam,” he answered, “you’ve already given me too much, and I’m afraid I was rude not to leave straight away. But if you’ll forgive me for saying so, I was struck dumb at finding such beautiful ladies on their own. A group of women without men, after all, is as dull as a group of men without women.” And after telling a few stories to prove his point, he ended by begging them to let him stay and make a fourth at their dinner.

The ladies found the man’s confident talk rather amusing, and after some discussion they agreed to let him stay, since his company might prove entertaining. “But listen, my friend,” said Zobeida. “We’ll grant your request only on condition that you behave with perfect politeness, and that you keep secret the way we live, which you have found out by chance.” Then they all sat down at the table, which Amina had laid with the dishes she had bought.

After the first few mouthfuls, Amina poured some wine into a golden cup. She drank first, as the Arab custom requires, and then filled it for her sisters. When it was the porter’s turn, he kissed Amina’s hand and sang a song he made up on the spot in praise of the wine. The three ladies liked the song and then sang some themselves, so the meal was a merry one and went on much longer than usual.
At last, seeing that the sun was about to set, Sadie said to the porter, “Get up and go. It’s time for us to part.”

“Oh, madam,” he replied, “how can you expect me to leave you in the state I’m in? Between the wine I’ve drunk and the joy of seeing you, I’d never find my way home. Let me stay here until morning, and when I’ve come to my senses I’ll go whenever you like.”
“Let him stay,” said Amina, who had already shown herself his friend. “It’s only fair, since he has given us so much amusement.”

“If you want it, sister,” Zobeida replied, “but if he stays, I must set a new condition. Porter,” she went on, turning to him, “if you stay, you must promise to ask no questions about anything you see. If you do, you may hear something you won’t like.”

With that settled, Amina brought in supper and lit the hall with a number of sweet-smelling candles. They sat down at the table again and began, with fresh appetite, to eat, drink, sing and recite verses. They were all enjoying themselves enormously when they heard a knock at the outer door, and Sadie got up to answer it. She soon came back to report that three Calenders, all blind in the right eye and all with their heads, faces and eyebrows shaved clean, were begging to be let in, since they had just arrived in Baghdad and night had already fallen. “They seem to have pleasant manners,” she added, “but you can’t imagine how funny they look. I’m sure their company would amuse us.”

Zobeida and Amina were reluctant to admit the newcomers, and Sadie knew why they hesitated. But she pressed her case so strongly that Zobeida finally had to give in. “Bring them in, then,” she said, “but make them understand that they must not comment on matters that are none of their business, and be sure they read the inscription over the door.” For on the door were written, in letters of gold, the words: “Whoever meddles in affairs that are none of his business will hear truths that will not please him.”

The three Calenders came in and bowed low, then thanked the ladies for their kindness and welcome. The ladies answered with warm greetings, and everyone was about to sit down when the Calenders noticed the porter. His clothes were not so very different from their own, except that he still had all the hair nature had given him. “That one,” said one of them, “looks like a fellow Arab of ours who has rebelled against our ruler.”

The porter was half asleep from the wine he had drunk, but he heard this. Without even stirring, he snapped at the Calender, “Sit down and mind your own business. Didn’t you read the inscription over the door? Not everyone has to live the same way.”

“Don’t be so angry, my good man,” the Calender replied. “We would be very sorry to offend you.” With that the quarrel was settled, and supper began in earnest. When the Calenders had eaten their fill, they offered to play for their hostesses if the house had any instruments. The ladies loved the idea. Sadie went to look and came back a few moments later carrying two kinds of flute and a tambourine. Each Calender took the one he liked best and began a well-known tune, while the ladies sang the words. The words were as merry and lively as could be, and every so often the singers had to stop and give way to the laughter that nearly choked them. In the middle of all this noise, there was a knock at the door.

Earlier that evening the Caliph had slipped out of his palace in secret, with his grand vizier Giafar and Mesrour, the chief of the eunuchs. All three were dressed as merchants. As they walked down the street, the Caliph had been drawn by the sound of instruments and laughter, and he had told his vizier to go and knock at the door of the house, because he wanted to go in. The vizier answered that the ladies who lived there seemed to be entertaining friends, and that his master would do well not to intrude. But the Caliph had made up his mind to see for himself, and he insisted on being obeyed.

Sadie answered the knock, holding a taper. The vizier was struck by her beauty and bowed low before her. “Madam,” he said respectfully, “we are three merchants who have just arrived from Moussoul. Because of a mishap that befell us tonight, we reached our inn only to find the doors shut against us until morning. We didn’t know what to do, so we wandered the streets until we happened to pass your house. Seeing lights and hearing voices, we decided to ask you for shelter until dawn. If you grant us this favor, then with your permission we will do everything we can to help you pass the time pleasantly.”

Sadie told the merchant she must first consult her sisters. After talking it over with them, she came back and told him that he and his two friends were welcome to join the party. They came in and bowed politely to the ladies and their guests. Then Zobeida, as the mistress of the house, stepped forward and said gravely, “You are welcome here, but I hope you will let me ask one thing of you. Have as many eyes as you like, but no tongues. Ask no questions about anything you see, however strange it may seem to you.”

“Madam,” the vizier answered, “you will be obeyed. We have plenty here to please and interest us, without troubling ourselves over matters that are none of our concern.” Then they all sat down and drank to the health of the new arrivals.

While Giafar the vizier chatted with the ladies, the Caliph kept wondering who they could be, and why each of the three Calenders had lost his right eye. He was burning to ask the reason behind it all, but Zobeida’s request kept him silent. So he made himself shake it off and join in the conversation, which was very lively; they were discussing the many different kinds of pleasure there are in the world. After a while the Calenders got up and performed some curious dances, which delighted the rest of the company.

When they had finished, Zobeida rose from her seat and took Amina by the hand. “Sister,” she said, “our friends will forgive us if we seem to forget they are here and do our nightly task.” Amina understood what her sister meant. She gathered up the dishes, glasses and musical instruments and carried them away, while Sadie swept the hall and put everything in order. When that was done, Sadie asked the Calenders to sit on a sofa on one side of the room, and the Caliph and his companions to sit opposite them. She asked the porter to come and help her and her sister.

A little later Amina came in carrying a seat, which she set down in the middle of the empty floor. Then she went to the door of a closet and signed to the porter to follow her. He did, and soon came back leading two black dogs on a chain, which he brought to the center of the hall. Zobeida rose from her place between the Calenders and the Caliph and walked slowly over to where the porter stood with the dogs. “We must do our duty,” she said with a deep sigh, pushing back her sleeves. She took a whip from Sadie and told the man, “Take one of those dogs to my sister Amina, and give me the other.”

The porter did as he was told, but as he led the dog to Zobeida it let out piercing howls and looked up at her with pleading eyes. Zobeida paid no attention. She whipped the dog until she was out of breath. Then she took the chain from the porter and lifted the dog onto its hind legs, and the two looked sorrowfully into each other’s eyes until tears began to fall from both. Zobeida took out her handkerchief and gently wiped the dog’s eyes, then kissed it. Putting the chain back into the porter’s hand, she said, “Take it back to the closet and bring me the other.”

The same ritual was repeated with the second dog, and the whole company watched in astonishment. The Caliph in particular could barely hold himself in, and he made signs to the vizier to ask what it all meant. But the vizier pretended not to notice and turned his head away.

Zobeida stayed in the middle of the room for some time, until Sadie went up to her and begged her to sit down, since Sadie too had a part to play. At this, Amina took a lute from a case of yellow satin and handed it to Sadie, who sang several songs to its music. When she grew tired, she said to Amina, “Sister, I can do no more. Please come and take my place.”

Amina struck a few chords and then burst into song. She sang with such passion that she was overcome and sank, gasping, onto a pile of cushions, tearing open her dress to get some air. To everyone’s amazement, her neck was not smooth and white like her face. It was a mass of scars.
The Calenders and the Caliph looked at one another and whispered together, where Zobeida and Sadie, busy tending their fainting sister, could not hear.
“What does it all mean?” asked the Caliph.
“We know no more than you do,” said the Calender he had spoken to.
“What! You don’t belong to the house?”
“My lord,” all the Calenders answered together, “we came here for the first time only an hour before you.”

Then they turned to the porter to see whether he could explain the mystery, but he was no wiser than they were. At last the Caliph could hold back his curiosity no longer. He declared that he would force the ladies to explain their strange behavior. The vizier saw what would come of it. He begged the Caliph to remember the condition their hostesses had set, and added in a whisper that if his Highness would only wait until morning, he could use his power as Caliph to summon the ladies before him. But the Caliph was not used to being contradicted and rejected this advice. After a little more discussion they agreed that the porter should put the question. Just then Zobeida turned round and saw how excited they were. “What is the matter?” she said. “What are you all discussing so earnestly?”

“Madam,” the porter answered, “these gentlemen beg you to tell them why you first whip the dogs and then cry over them, and also how the fainting lady came to be covered with scars. They have asked me, Madam, to speak for them.”
“Is it true, gentlemen,” Zobeida asked, drawing herself up, “that you have told this man to put that question to me?”
“It is,” they all replied, except Giafar, who stayed silent.

“Is this,” Zobeida went on, growing angrier by the moment, “is this how you repay the hospitality I have shown you? Have you forgotten the one condition on which you were allowed into this house? Come quickly,” she added, clapping her hands three times. The words were hardly out of her mouth when seven black slaves, each armed with a sabre, burst in. They stood over the seven men, threw them to the ground, and got ready to cut off their heads at a sign from their mistress.

The seven culprits all thought their last hour had come, and the Caliph bitterly regretted not taking the vizier’s advice. But they resolved to die bravely, all except the porter. He asked Zobeida loudly why he should suffer for other people’s faults. He declared that none of this would have happened if not for the Calenders, who always brought bad luck. He ended by begging Zobeida not to confuse the innocent with the guilty, and to spare his life.

Angry as she was, there was something so comical in the porter’s groans that Zobeida could not help laughing. But she set him aside and spoke to the others again. “Answer me. Who are you? Unless you tell me the truth, you have not another moment to live. I can hardly believe you are men of any standing, whatever country you come from. If you were, you would have shown us more consideration.”

The Caliph was naturally impatient, and he suffered far more than the others at the thought that his life lay at the mercy of a lady he had rightly offended. But when he heard her question, he began to breathe more easily, convinced that she had only to learn his name and rank for all danger to vanish. So he whispered hurriedly to the vizier beside him, telling him to reveal their secret. The vizier was wiser than his master and wanted to keep the insult they had received from becoming public. He only answered, “After all, we have got no more than we deserved.”
Meanwhile Zobeida had turned to the three Calenders and asked whether they were brothers, since they were all blind.
“No, madam,” one of them replied, “we are no relations by blood at all, only brothers by the way we live.”
“And you,” she asked, speaking to another, “were you born blind in one eye?”

“No, madam,” he answered, “I lost my eye through a most astonishing adventure, the like of which has probably never happened to anyone. After that I shaved my head and eyebrows and put on the clothes you see me wearing now.”
Zobeida asked the other two Calenders the same thing, and both gave her the same reply.
“But,” added the third, “you may be interested to know, madam, that we are not men of low birth. All three of us are sons of kings, and kings the world holds in high esteem.”

At these words Zobeida’s anger cooled. She turned to her slaves and said, “You may give them a little more freedom, but do not leave the hall. Those who tell us their histories and their reasons for coming here will be allowed to leave unharmed. Those who refuse—” She paused. But the porter understood that all he had to do to be free of this terrible danger was tell his story, and he broke in at once.

“Madam, you already know how I came here, and what I have to say will take no time. Your sister found me this morning in the place where I always stand waiting to be hired. She told me to follow her to various shops, and when my basket was full we came back to this house. You were kind enough to let me stay, and I will be grateful for it forever. That is my story.”
He looked anxiously at Zobeida, who nodded and said, “You may go. And make sure we never meet again.”

“Oh, madam,” cried the porter, “let me stay a little longer. It isn’t fair that the others should have heard my story and I shouldn’t hear theirs.” Without waiting for permission he sat down at the end of the sofa where the ladies were sitting, while the rest crouched on the carpet and the slaves stood against the wall.
Then one of the Calenders turned to Zobeida, as the chief lady, and began his story.
